wiki_fulltext:
Dasyuromorphia ( da-see-yoor-oh-MOR-fee-ə) is an order comprising most of the Australian carnivorous marsupials. The order contains four families: Myrmecobiidae, with just a single living species, the numbat (Myrmecobius fasciatus); Thylacinidae, with one recently extinct species, the thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus) and several fossil species; Dasyuridae, with 73 extant species, including quolls, dunnarts, and the Tasmanian devil; and the extinct fossil family Malleodectidae with six genera.


Description
The body size of dasyuromorphs varies considerably, from only 4 grams (0.14 oz) in long-tailed planigale, which is the smallest living marsupial, up to 35 kilograms (77 lb) in the recently extinct thylacine (Thylacinus cynocephalus). They show considerable morphological diversity, including the kultarr (Antechinomys laniger), which is adapted for hopping locomotion. Members of the group are mostly carnivorous, either feeding on vertebrate prey or arthropods such as insects. The lower molar teeth of dasyuromorphs typically show a carnassial-like morphology. Members of this order are monophyodont, meaning they only have one set of teeth throughout their lives. Each erupting molar must function as a carnassial, before being pushed forward in the jaw by the next erupting molar. Because of this, dasyuromorphs are prevented from adapting some molars for other functions, which may have restricted their diversity relative to carnivorans.

grok_lead: Dasyuromorphia is an order of carnivorous and insectivorous marsupials primarily native to Australia, New Guinea, Tasmania, and surrounding islands, encompassing a diverse radiation of approximately 75 extant species characterized by their faunivorous diets, nocturnal or crepuscular habits, and specialized reproductive strategies. The order is classified within the subclass Marsupialia and superorder Australidelphia, comprising three families: Dasyuridae (the largest, including quolls, dunnarts, and the Tasmanian devil, with about 70 species across 20 genera), Myrmecobiidae (represented solely by the numbat, Myrmecobius fasciatus, a diurnal termite specialist), and the extinct Thylacinidae (formerly including the thylacine or Tasmanian tiger, Thylacinus cynocephalus, officially declared extinct by the IUCN in 1982). These marsupials exhibit a wide range of body sizes, from the tiny 10-gram fat-tailed dunnart ( Sminthopsis crassicaudata) to the 12-kilogram Tasmanian devil ( Sarcophilus harrisii), with males typically larger than females due to sexual dimorphism. Geographically, dasyuromorphs are endemic to Australasia, inhabiting diverse environments from arid deserts and savannas to temperate forests, rainforests, and montane regions, though many species face threats from habitat loss, introduced predators, and climate change. Behaviorally, most are solitary and predatory, relying on acute senses for hunting small vertebrates, invertebrates, and occasionally carrion, with communication via scent marking, vocalizations, and visual displays; the numbat stands out as a diurnal exception, foraging openly for termites and ants, consuming up to 20,000 individuals daily. Reproduction in Dasyuromorphia is polyestrous or seasonally restricted, with short gestation periods (9â40 days) followed by development in a forward-opening pouch; many dasyurids exhibit semelparity, where males die after a single intense breeding season due to stress-induced immune suppression, while females provide sole parental care. Evolutionarily, the order traces back to the late Oligocene (about 26â28 million years ago) based on fossil evidence from Australia, with adaptive radiations filling carnivorous niches left vacant by placental mammals in the region; phylogenetic analyses confirm monophyly of the order, supported by both molecular and morphological data. Notable conservation concerns include the vulnerability of species like the northern quoll ( Dasyurus hallucatus) to cane toad invasion and ongoing efforts to protect the numbat through reintroduction programs, alongside de-extinction research for the thylacine as of 2025.
